To put it more pithily: the casting of Bette Midler as Sue Mengers is genius.
Midler's consummate ability to deliver brassy chutzpah, fierceness and silky comic seduction at the same time is harnessed to perfection, allowing just a judicious whisper of vulnerability.

It’s a heady sensation, thanks to the buoyant, witty writing of Mr. Logan (“Red”), the focused direction of Joe Mantello and above all to Ms. Midler, who gives the most lusciously entertaining performance of the Broadway season.
Which, despite the expert attention of director Joe Mantello, is what I’ll Eat You Last would do without Midler.
There will be some for whom 90 minutes in the presence of an outsize character playing an outsize character will be a most delightful evening, leaving ample time for post-show martinis.
“I’ll Eat You Last” is wickedly entertaining precisely because performer and material are so perfectly matched.
But the play itself feels more like an extended celebrity impression than a fully realized theatrical experience.
Midler manages a fabulous feat: She marshals all her own famously divine Bette-ness to bring to life a kindred spirit.
Midler reminds us what a strong dramatic actress she can be, whether evoking Mengers' challenges or showing us the moxie that got her through them.
As the monologue grows in texture, Midler shines, serving less of a caricature and more of a person--someone who it turns out has some real feeling lurking beneath the caftan and the zingers.
Midler is a riot simply sitting still and dishing the dirt.
But in light of this rare opportunity to catch Midler onstage, a more substantial meal would have been nice instead of 90 minutes of pure dessert.
Thanks to the lazy writing and acting, Mengers goes missing.
Those who come knowing Midler but not Mengers (who died in 2011) will be disappointed by this weightless valedictory, for there’s no swan, and no song.

cn.t: Critics find Midler's star power elevates Logan's lightweight script about legendary agent Sue Mengers, though the one-woman show offers more gossip and glitz than dramatic substance.

sg.ra: The Booth is one of Broadway's smallest houses at 766 seats, so center orchestra rows C-H give close-up detail of plays and intimate dramas without paying the very-front premium. Row AA front offers max legroom (Headout) but stage is high; step back a few rows for better sightline onto the stage floor.

sg.vl: Workable angle, not the sweet spot
sg.ra: Booth is narrow so side orchestra remains viable, but a 2018 BWW forum post specifically flagged 'angle from the front side seats' as a concern. Closer rows (BB, A) on the side get awkward angles onto the high stage. Mid-house aisle seats recover the view while adding legroom.
sg.rr: A-P (17 rows, odd 1-15 left, even 2-16 right)

sg.ra: In a 252-seat mezzanine with only 8 rows, even the back row is close. SeatPlan and Headout both call Center Mezz A-B some of the best seats in the house, and G-H are cited as strong value. With the Booth's intimate scale, the mezzanine never feels distant — this is the value pick.

sg.vl: Small house saves the side angle
sg.ra: SeatPlan explicitly notes side-mezz views are 'slightly more angled but still viable' because the Booth is narrow. Decent budget alternative, but the center mezz is a better value at similar price tier so this is solid-not-sweet.
